name: Chapter 10: Thermal Properties of Matter
description: Temperature scales, ideal gas, thermal expansion, specific heat, calorimetry, change of state, latent heat, conduction, convection, radiation, Newton’s cooling

cards.term: Temperature vs heat?
cards.definition: Temperature: measure of hotness (K, °C). Heat: energy transferred because of a temperature difference (J)

cards.term: Why is touch not a good thermometer?
cards.definition: It is unreliable and its range is too limited

cards.term: Any energy transfer without a temperature difference: is it heat?
cards.definition: No (e.g. work done by stirring is not heat)

cards.term: Why does a temperature scale need fixed points?
cards.definition: All substances expand, so there is no absolute reference; we use phenomena that always happen at the same temperature (ice point, steam point)

cards.term: Ice and steam points on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales?
cards.definition: Celsius: 0 °C, 100 °C (100 divisions). Fahrenheit: 32 °F, 212 °F (180 divisions)

cards.term: Celsius–Fahrenheit conversion?
At what temperature do Celsius and Fahrenheit readings agree?
cards.definition: −40° (solve x = 9x/5 + 32)

cards.term: Teacher addition: general rule to convert between any two linear scales?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{X - L}{U - L} \) is the same on every scale (L = lower, U = upper fixed point)

cards.term: Boyle’s law and Charles’ law?
cards.definition: Boyle (T constant): PV = constant. Charles (P constant): V/T = constant

cards.term: Ideal gas equation?
cards.definition: \( PV = \mu RT \), R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, μ = number of moles

cards.term: Why is a gas thermometer better than a liquid-in-glass one?
cards.definition: All low-density gases expand the same way, so a gas thermometer reads the same whichever gas is used

cards.term: Constant-volume gas thermometer: what is read?
cards.definition: Pressure: at constant V, P ∝ T

cards.term: How is absolute zero found?
cards.definition: Extrapolate P–T lines of low-density gases to P = 0: all meet at −273.15 °C

cards.term: Kelvin–Celsius relation?
cards.definition: \( T = t_C + 273.15 \); one kelvin = one Celsius degree

cards.term: Absolute zero in °F?
cards.definition: −459.67 °F (NCERT’s Fig. 10.4 prints −459.69 °F; the accepted value is −459.67 °F)

cards.term: Why is the triple point of water the modern fixed point (Exercise 10.4a)?
cards.definition: It has a unique temperature (273.16 K); melting and boiling points depend on pressure

cards.term: Why is T = tc + 273.15 and not + 273.16 (Exercise 10.4c)?
cards.definition: The triple point is 0.01 °C = 273.16 K; the melting point of ice (0 °C) is 273.15 K

cards.term: Exercise 10.4(d): triple point of water on an absolute scale with Fahrenheit-sized degrees?
Exercise 10.2: absolute scales A and B give the triple point as 200 A and 350 B. Relation?
cards.definition: \( T_A = \tfrac47 T_B \)

cards.term: Exercise 10.3: R = 101.6 Ω at 273.16 K, 165.5 Ω at 600.5 K (linear). Temperature when R = 123.4 Ω?
cards.definition: ≈ 384.8 K

cards.term: Exercise 10.5: why do oxygen and hydrogen gas thermometers disagree slightly? Remedy?
cards.definition: Real gases are not perfectly ideal. Take readings at lower and lower pressures and extrapolate to P → 0

cards.term: Why does dipping a tight metal lid in hot water help open a bottle?
cards.definition: The metal lid expands more than the glass

cards.term: Three kinds of thermal expansion?
cards.definition: Linear (length), area, volume

cards.term: Coefficient of linear expansion?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \alpha_l\,\Delta T \)

cards.term: Table 10.1: αₗ of copper vs glass (pyrex)?
cards.definition: Copper 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ vs pyrex 0.32 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹: copper expands about 5 times more

cards.term: Coefficient of volume expansion?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \alpha_V\,\Delta T \); not strictly constant — depends on temperature

cards.term: Relations between αₗ, αA and αV (isotropic solid)?
cards.definition: \( \alpha_A = 2\alpha_l,\quad \alpha_V = 3\alpha_l \)

cards.term: Coefficient of area expansion = 2αl
cards.definition: ΔA = aΔb + bΔa + ΔaΔb = αl A ΔT (2 + αl ΔT) ≈ 2αl A ΔT

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 10.1 · area expansion

Find the missing step.

Show that the coefficient of area expansion of a rectangular sheet is 2αₗ.
  1. Δa = αₗaΔT, Δb = αₗbΔT
  2. ΔA = aΔb + bΔa + ΔaΔb
  3. ?
  4. αₗΔT ≪ 2, so ΔA/A = 2αₗΔT
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 10.1 · area expansion

Find the missing step.

Show that the coefficient of area expansion of a rectangular sheet is 2αₗ.
  1. Δa = αₗaΔT, Δb = αₗbΔT
  2. ΔA = aΔb + bΔa + ΔaΔb
  3. = αₗAΔT(2 + αₗΔT)
  4. αₗΔT ≪ 2, so ΔA/A = 2αₗΔT

cards.term: Identify: which strips make up the extra area in Fig. 10.8?
cards.definition: ΔA₁ = aΔb, ΔA₂ = bΔa and the tiny corner ΔaΔb (neglected)

cards.term: Which have very low expansion: name two.
cards.definition: Invar (iron–nickel alloy, αV ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and pyrex glass

cards.term: Which expands more for the same rise: alcohol or mercury?
cards.definition: Alcohol (αV ≈ 110 × 10⁻⁵ vs 18.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹)

cards.term: Anomalous expansion of water?
cards.definition: Water contracts on heating from 0 °C to 4 °C; density is maximum at 4 °C

cards.term: Why do lakes freeze from the top, and why does it matter?
cards.definition: Water below 4 °C is less dense and stays on top where it freezes; the water underneath stays near 4 °C, so aquatic life survives

cards.term: Volume expansivity of an ideal gas at constant pressure?
cards.definition: \( \alpha_V = \dfrac1T \) (≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹ at 0 °C) — far larger than for solids and liquids

cards.term: What is thermal stress?
cards.definition: Stress in a body prevented from expanding: strain = αΔT, stress = YαΔT

cards.term: Steel rail (40 cm², α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) fixed at both ends, heated 10 °C. Thermal stress and force?
cards.definition: Stress = 2.4 × 10⁷ Pa; force ≈ 10⁵ N — enough to bend rails (hence gaps between rails)

cards.term: Example 10.2: iron ring 5.231 m fits a 5.243 m wooden rim at 27 °C. To what temperature must the ring be heated?
cards.definition: ≈ 218 °C

cards.term: Exercise 10.7: steel shaft 8.70 cm, wheel hole 8.69 cm at 27 °C. Cool the shaft to what temperature?
cards.definition: ≈ −69 °C

cards.term: Exercise 10.8: a hole of 4.24 cm in a copper sheet, heated from 27 °C to 227 °C. Change in diameter?
cards.definition: Increases by 1.44 × 10⁻² cm: a hole expands like the material around it

cards.term: Exercise 10.9: brass wire 1.8 m, 2.0 mm diameter, held taut and cooled from 27 °C to −39 °C. Tension?
cards.definition: F = YAαΔT ≈ 3.8 × 10² N

cards.term: Exercise 10.10: brass and steel rods (50 cm each) joined, heated 40 → 250 °C, ends free. Change in length? Thermal stress?
cards.definition: 0.34 cm total; no thermal stress (free to expand)

cards.term: Exercise 10.11: fractional change in density of glycerine (αV = 49 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) for a 30 °C rise?
cards.definition: ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻² decrease (Δρ/ρ ≈ −αVΔT)

cards.term: Exercise 10.6: a steel tape calibrated at 27 °C reads 63.0 cm at 45 °C. Actual length that day?
cards.definition: 63.0136 cm (≈ 63.0 cm to 3 s.f.)

cards.term: Heat needed to warm a substance depends on…?
cards.definition: Mass, temperature change and the nature of the substance

cards.term: Define heat capacity and specific heat capacity.
cards.definition: \( S = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T} \) ; \( s = \dfrac{1}{m}\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T} \) (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

cards.term: Define molar specific heat capacity.
cards.definition: \( C = \dfrac{1}{\mu}\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T} \) (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

cards.term: Why do gases have two molar specific heats?
cards.definition: Heat can be supplied at constant pressure (Cₚ) or constant volume (Cᵥ); Cₚ > Cᵥ

cards.term: Which common substance has the highest specific heat? Value?
cards.definition: Water: 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

cards.term: Uses and effects of water’s high specific heat?
cards.definition: Coolant in car radiators, hot-water bags; sea warms slowly, so sea breeze cools the coast; deserts heat and cool quickly

cards.term: Exercise 10.15: why are Cᵥ values of diatomic gases (~5 cal/mol K) higher than monatomic (2.92)? Chlorine is higher still.
cards.definition: Diatomic molecules also store energy in rotation (Cᵥ ≈ 5R/2); chlorine’s vibrational modes are active too

cards.text: Principle of calorimetry: in an isolated system, {{c1::heat lost by the hotter part = heat gained by the colder part}}.

cards.term: Construction of a calorimeter?
cards.definition: Copper/aluminium vessel and stirrer inside a wooden jacket with insulating material (glass wool); thermometer through the lid

cards.term: Specific heat of aluminium by mixtures
cards.definition: Heat lost by Al = heat gained by water + calorimeter → s ≈ 0.911 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 10.3 · aluminium sphere

Find the missing step.

0.047 kg Al at 100 °C dropped into 0.25 kg water + 0.14 kg copper calorimeter at 20 °C; final 23 °C. s(Al)?
  1. Heat lost by Al = 0.047 × s × 77
  2. ?
  3. ≈ 3297 J
  4. s(Al) = 3297 / (0.047 × 77) ≈ 911 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 10.3 · aluminium sphere

Find the missing step.

0.047 kg Al at 100 °C dropped into 0.25 kg water + 0.14 kg copper calorimeter at 20 °C; final 23 °C. s(Al)?
  1. Heat lost by Al = 0.047 × s × 77
  2. Heat gained = (0.25 × 4180 + 0.14 × 386) × 3
  3. ≈ 3297 J
  4. s(Al) = 3297 / (0.047 × 77) ≈ 911 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

cards.term: Exercise 10.14: 0.20 kg metal at 150 °C into water (150 g) + calorimeter (water equivalent 25 g) at 27 °C; final 40 °C. s? Effect of heat loss?
cards.definition: 0.43 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; with losses, the calculated value is smaller than the true value

cards.term: Exercise 10.12: 10 kW drill, half the power heats an 8.0 kg aluminium block (0.91 J/g K) for 2.5 min. Temperature rise?
cards.definition: ≈ 103 °C

cards.term: Exercise 10.13: 2.5 kg copper at 500 °C on a large ice block. Maximum ice melted?
cards.definition: ≈ 1.5 kg

cards.term: Temperature of ice being heated while it melts?
cards.definition: Stays constant (0 °C) until all the ice melts; the heat goes into changing state

cards.term: Define melting point.
cards.definition: The temperature at which solid and liquid coexist in equilibrium; depends on pressure. At 1 atm: normal melting point

cards.term: What is regelation? Example?
cards.definition: Ice melts under pressure (below a loaded wire) and refreezes when the pressure is removed; the wire passes through without splitting the slab. Also makes skating possible

cards.term: Define boiling point; effect of pressure?
cards.definition: Liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium; boiling point rises with pressure

cards.term: Why is cooking hard on hills but fast in a pressure cooker?
cards.definition: Lower pressure on hills → lower boiling point; a pressure cooker raises pressure → higher boiling point

cards.term: What is sublimation? Examples?
cards.definition: Solid → vapour directly: dry ice (solid CO₂), iodine

cards.term: What is the triple point? Water’s?
cards.definition: Where solid, liquid and vapour coexist (sublimation, fusion and vaporisation curves meet). Water: 273.16 K, 0.006 atm

cards.term: Correction: NCERT’s box gives the triple-point pressure of water as 6.11 × 10⁻³ Pa. What is right?
cards.definition: 611 Pa = 6.11 × 10⁻³ bar ≈ 0.006 atm (as its own phase diagram shows). The book wrote Pa where it meant bar

cards.term: Fusion curve of water vs CO₂: slope?
cards.definition: Water: negative slope (melting point falls with pressure — regelation). CO₂: positive; at 1 atm CO₂ sublimes (triple point 5.11 atm)

cards.term: Define latent heat.
cards.definition: \( Q = mL \): heat per unit mass for a change of state at constant temperature (J kg⁻¹)

cards.term: Latent heats of water?
cards.definition: Fusion Lf = 3.33 × 10⁵ J/kg; vaporisation Lv = 22.6 × 10⁵ J/kg

cards.term: Why do steam burns hurt more than boiling-water burns?
cards.definition: Steam at 100 °C carries an extra 22.6 × 10⁵ J/kg of latent heat

cards.term: In the temperature–heat graph of water, why do the sloping parts differ in slope?
cards.definition: Slope ∝ 1/(ms): ice, water and steam have different specific heats

cards.term: Example 10.4: 0.15 kg ice at 0 °C + 0.30 kg water at 50 °C → 6.7 °C. Lf?
cards.definition: 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg

cards.term: Ice at −12 °C to steam at 100 °C
cards.definition: Four stages add to about 9.1 × 10⁶ J

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 10.5 · ice to steam

Find the missing step.

Heat to turn 3 kg of ice at −12 °C into steam at 100 °C?
  1. Ice −12 → 0 °C: 3 × 2100 × 12 = 75 600 J
  2. Melt: 3 × 3.35 × 10⁵ = 1 005 000 J
  3. ?
  4. Boil: 3 × 2.256 × 10⁶ = 6 768 000 J → total ≈ 9.1 × 10⁶ J
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 10.5 · ice to steam

Find the missing step.

Heat to turn 3 kg of ice at −12 °C into steam at 100 °C?
  1. Ice −12 → 0 °C: 3 × 2100 × 12 = 75 600 J
  2. Melt: 3 × 3.35 × 10⁵ = 1 005 000 J
  3. Water 0 → 100 °C: 3 × 4186 × 100 = 1 255 800 J
  4. Boil: 3 × 2.256 × 10⁶ = 6 768 000 J → total ≈ 9.1 × 10⁶ J

cards.term: Mnemonic for the ice-to-steam heating curve?
cards.definition: "Slope, flat, slope, flat, slope": heat (s), melt (Lf), heat (s), boil (Lv), heat (s)

cards.term: Exercise 10.16: a child (30 kg) cools from 101 °F to 98 °F in 20 min by sweating (L = 580 cal/g). Rate of evaporation?
cards.definition: ≈ 4.3 g/min

cards.term: Three modes of heat transfer?
cards.definition: Conduction, convection, radiation

cards.term: What is conduction?
cards.definition: Heat transfer between neighbouring parts of a body through molecular collisions, without bulk flow of matter

cards.term: Rate of heat flow through a bar in steady state?
cards.definition: \( H = KA\dfrac{T_C - T_D}{L} \) (K = thermal conductivity, W m⁻¹ K⁻¹)

cards.term: Table 10.6: best and worst conductors?
cards.definition: Silver 406, copper 385 W/m K; air 0.024, glass wool 0.04

cards.term: Why do cooking pots have copper bottoms, and why are plastic foams good insulators?
cards.definition: Copper spreads heat evenly (large K); foams trap pockets of air (very small K)

cards.term: Why is a layer of earth or foam put on concrete roofs?
cards.definition: Concrete’s K is not small enough; the layer insulates and keeps rooms cool

cards.term: Example 10.6: steel (15 cm, area 2A, K = 50.2) and copper (10 cm, area A, K = 385) in series, 300 °C to 0 °C. Junction temperature?
cards.definition: ≈ 44.4 °C

cards.term: Example 10.7: iron (K = 79) and brass (K = 109) bars of equal size in series, 373 K to 273 K. Junction temperature, K(equivalent)?
cards.definition: T₀ = 315 K; K′ = 2K₁K₂/(K₁ + K₂) = 91.6 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹; H ≈ 916 W

cards.term: Teacher addition: thermal resistance and bars in series/parallel?
cards.definition: \( R_{th} = \dfrac{L}{KA} \); in series resistances add, in parallel their reciprocals add (like resistors)

cards.term: Exercise 10.17: thermacole icebox (30 cm cube, walls 5 cm, K = 0.01), 4 kg ice, outside 45 °C, 6 h. Ice left?
cards.definition: ≈ 3.7 kg

cards.term: Exercise 10.18: brass boiler base 0.15 m², 1.0 cm thick, boils 6.0 kg/min. Flame temperature?
cards.definition: ≈ 238 °C

cards.term: Exercise 10.19(b): why does a brass tumbler feel colder than a wooden tray on a chilly day?
cards.definition: Brass is a good conductor: it draws heat from your hand quickly

cards.term: What is convection? Where is it possible?
cards.definition: Heat transfer by actual bulk motion of matter; only in fluids

cards.term: Natural vs forced convection? Examples?
cards.definition: Natural: driven by gravity/buoyancy (sea breeze). Forced: by a pump or fan (house heating, blood circulation, car cooling system)

cards.term: Sea breeze and land breeze?
cards.definition: Day: land heats faster, warm air rises over land, cool air flows in from the sea (sea breeze). Night: reversed (land breeze)

cards.term: What are trade winds?
cards.definition: Steady surface winds blowing from the north-east towards the equator: convection modified by Earth’s rotation; air descends near 30° N

cards.term: A hot bar under a running tap loses heat mainly by…?
cards.definition: Conduction between the bar and water, not convection within the water

cards.term: Exercise 10.19(e): why is steam heating more efficient than hot-water heating?
cards.definition: Condensing steam releases a large latent heat per kg

cards.term: What is thermal radiation? Why needs no medium?
cards.definition: Electromagnetic waves emitted because of temperature; EM waves travel through vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m/s

cards.term: Why wear white clothes in summer and dark ones in winter?
cards.definition: Dark bodies absorb and emit radiation better; white reflects the Sun’s heat

cards.term: How does a thermos (Dewar) flask reduce heat transfer?
cards.definition: Silvered walls (radiation), vacuum between walls (conduction, convection), cork support

cards.term: State Wien’s displacement law.
cards.definition: \( \lambda_m T = b \), b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K

cards.term: Why does heated iron glow dull red, then yellow, then white?
cards.definition: As T rises, λₘ shifts to shorter wavelengths (Wien)

cards.term: Surface temperatures of the Moon and Sun from Wien’s law?
cards.definition: Moon: λₘ ≈ 14 μm → ≈ 200 K. Sun: λₘ = 4753 Å → ≈ 6000 K (surface, not interior)

cards.term: State the Stefan–Boltzmann law.
cards.definition: \( H = Ae\sigma T^4 \), σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, e = emissivity (1 for a perfect radiator)

cards.term: Net radiation loss of a body at T in surroundings at Tₛ?
cards.definition: \( H = e\sigma A\,(T^4 - T_s^4) \)

cards.term: Heat radiated by a person (1.9 m², skin 28 °C, room 22 °C, e = 0.97)?
cards.definition: ≈ 66 W — over half the body’s resting output (120 W); arctic clothing adds a shiny reflecting layer

cards.term: Exercise 10.19(a): why is a good reflector a poor emitter?
cards.definition: Good reflectors are poor absorbers, and good absorbers are good emitters

cards.term: Exercise 10.19(d): why would Earth be very cold without its atmosphere?
cards.definition: The atmosphere traps the Earth’s infrared radiation (greenhouse effect)

cards.term: State Newton’s law of cooling.
cards.definition: \( -\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = k(T_2 - T_1) \): rate of heat loss ∝ excess temperature over the surroundings (small differences only)

cards.term: Temperature of a cooling body with time?
cards.definition: \( T_2 = T_1 + Ce^{-Kt} \), K = k/ms: an exponential decay of the excess temperature

cards.term: How is Newton’s law of cooling verified?
cards.definition: Plot ln(T₂ − T₁) against t: a straight line with negative slope

cards.term: Teacher addition: average form of Newton’s law used in problems?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} = K\left(\bar T - T_s\right) \) (use the average temperature over the interval)

cards.term: Example 10.8: food cools 94 → 86 °C in 2 min (room 20 °C). Time for 71 → 69 °C?
cards.definition: 8/2 = K(70) and 2/t = K(50) → t = 0.7 min = 42 s

cards.term: Exercise 10.20: a body cools 80 → 50 °C in 5 min (room 20 °C). Time for 60 → 30 °C?
cards.definition: 9 min

cards.term: Chapter 10 formula sheet
cards.definition: Linear expansion: Δl = αₗ l ΔT; αV and αₗ: αV = 3αₗ; Heat for temperature change: Q = ms ΔT; Heat for change of state: Q = mL; Conduction: H = KA ΔT / L; Radiation: H = eσAT⁴

cards.term: Chapter 10 concept checks
cards.definition: Melting and boiling points of water are exactly 0 °C and 100 °C today: False (very close); Two phases in equilibrium have the same density: False (same P and T); Heat transfer always involves a temperature difference: True

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

Two phases in equilibrium have the same density?
Heat transfer always involves a temperature difference?
